title: SparkLend's kinked interest rate curve is a self-correcting control loop around a target utilization
content:
The Interest Rate Model has four inputs (A.6.1.1.1.3.2.1.1.1.3): a **Base Rate** at 0% utilization, **Variable Slope 1** — the rate at optimal utilization (.1.15) — **Variable Slope 2** — the rate at 100% utilization (.1.17) — and utilization itself. Optimal utilization is defined as "the desired target utilization," with the explicit behaviour that "when the actual utilization is above the optimal utilization, borrowing rates will be higher; and when the actual utilization is below the optimal utilization, borrowing rates will be lower" (.1.11).

The kink at optimal utilization is what makes this a controller rather than a price schedule. Below target, rates stay in the gentle Base-to-Slope-1 band and borrowing is cheap, drawing demand in. Above target, the curve turns steeply toward Slope 2, and the rising rate simultaneously pushes borrowers to repay and pulls suppliers in — two corrective forces from one parameter.

The quantity being defended is **withdrawal liquidity**. In a pooled lending market, utilization at 100% means no supplier can withdraw; the steep second slope exists to make full utilization so expensive that it is transient. Setting Slope 2 high is not a revenue decision, it is a solvency-of-redemption decision.

This is the same control philosophy as the Spark Liquidity Layer's `slope` rate limits: bound the dangerous state by making approach to it progressively costly, rather than by hard-blocking at a threshold. Both prefer a gradient to a cliff, so the system degrades smoothly instead of stopping.
description: Rates rise gently to Slope 1 at optimal utilization then steeply to Slope 2 at 100%, so the curve pushes borrowing and supply back toward target without anyone intervening.
